subject: [PATCH v3 0/6] btrfs: handle -ENOMEM errors in some synchronous dirops without aborting

reviews.author: Qu Wenruo
reviews.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch does not handle ENOMEM errors in all synchronous directory operations, specifically mentioning btrfs_create_new_inode() and btrfs_del_orphan_item(), and requested further work to address these cases.

2026-08-13.patch_summary: This patchset addresses a long-standing issue in the Btrfs file system where memory allocation failures can cause an abort during synchronous directory operations. The patches rework the code to perform allocations upfront, before reaching the point of potential aborts. This approach is designed to work in conjunction with another series that aims to prevent new memory allocations from triggering ENOMEM errors. Although this patchset does not cover all possible cases where ENOMEM can occur, it provides a significant improvement over the current state and is intended as an intermediate step towards fully addressing the issue.

reviews.author: David Sterba
reviews.summary: Reviewer David Sterba expressed concern about excessive stack usage in the patch, citing a potential trade-off between allocation failure and stack consumption. He suggested arguing for the chosen stack size in the changelog and exploring alternative memory allocation strategies such as using __GFP_HIGH.
reviews.raw_body:
112 is too much for on-stack, we've avoided that for btrfs_path in
particular, except some justified cases. This means in general the
beginning of call stack like ioctl, syscall handler and such. Otherwise
we assume there are other layers in the IO stack, like block device
drivers (DM), NFS, encoding layers or networking (iscsi), and obviously
the lowest level device drivers.

The trade off with possible allocation failure vs stack consumption
needs to be argued in the changelog, "is just 112" is not sufficient.

Getting back the consumed stack space is painful, we've been reducing
unneeded or redundant parameters of functions for years. The gains are
like -8 bytes here and -8 bytes there, allocation of +112 wipes that out.

If the place of allocation is critical we can consider that but we have
too many of them, anywhere during the transaction commit path or
irreversible metadata changes. Possibly using __GFP_HIGH could work, but
I haven't explored that.

Qu added the patches to for-next but I had no chance to look closely at
this patchset yet and am hesitant to leave it like that.

reviews.author: Jeff Layton (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledges that the allocation can fail due to deep stack sizes, but believes it's justified given the potential consequences of aborting the fs. The author is interested in hearing Qu Wenruo's take on this approach.
reviews.raw_body:
Fair critique. These days I think we're mostly ~16k stacks, but it can
certainly get deep given the right layering.

In this case, failing this allocation can lead to aborting the fs, so
it seemed justified. This is a GFP_NOFS allocation too, so it can
easily fail, even though it's small.

Qu suggested this approach in an earlier review pass, so I'd be
interested to hear his take on this too.

Thanks for taking a look!
-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

reviews.author: Qu Wenruo
reviews.summary:
Qu Wenruo pointed out that the patch's author is inconsistent in their use of on-stack memory allocation, having previously added 128 bytes for huge page support but being hesitant to remove similar allocations elsewhere. Qu requested data on on-stack memory usage and argued that the extra 112 bytes could cause problems with deep storage stacks.

The reviewer agrees with the patch but suggests additional context would be helpful, specifically a good call trace showing the issue causing a read-only (RO) flip in metadata
reviews.raw_body:
I think you're very inconsistent on on-stack memory usage at least.

You were fine when I was adding 128bytes for several call sites for the 
support of huge pages, and I'd argue all those call sites have a deeper 
stack, because it's on the writeback path.

Furthermore, that huge page support is not widely used, but everyone 
will need to pay that on-stack price.

On the other hand, you are also very hesitant on my recent patches 
removing those 128 bytes usages.

So your behavior doesn't seem to match what you said here.


Secondly, your deep-in-the-stack argument doesn't sound solid either.

Every block file system can be built upon layer of storage stacks, not 
only btrfs, but *every* block fs as long as there is a chance to do IO.
This means you're just saying, there can be almost-infinite lower layers 
under us, so we should not use any extra on-stack memory.

I do not think this is the sane nor really validated.

If you want to argue if the extra 112 bytes is good or not, give me some 
data about the on-stack memory usage.
With the proof that with enough stacked dm layer, that extra 112 bytes 
are going to cause problem.

Not to mention I believe some dm drivers are queuing the real submission 
handling into a workqueue, avoiding further increasing the on-stack 
memory usage.

---

Although I agree that more changelog will help, especially if Jeff has a 
good call trace showing that this is causing a flip RO in meta's fleet.

reviews.author: Qu Wenruo
reviews.summary: Reviewer Qu Wenruo expressed concern about the inconsistent handling of on-stack memory allocation in the patchset, specifically requesting a more consistent approach to on-stack memory usage.
reviews.raw_body:
For now I have removed those from for-next, but I really hope you can 
come up with a consistent behavior on on-stack memory usage.

reviews.author: Jeff Layton (author)
reviews.summary: The author is addressing Qu Wenruo's concern about the potential -ENOMEM failure in btrfs_orphan_add(). The author explains that they added patches to fix this issue based on LLM review and Qu's recommendation, but now suggests dropping those patches if there's no evidence of the problem. They provide analysis from an LLM showing that ENOMEM aborts do not occur in btrfs_orphan_add(), and instead happen in other functions such as btrfs_rename().
sentiment_signals: author acknowledges a fix is needed
reviews.raw_body:
No. I don't have any evidence of btrfs_orphan_add() failing because of
-ENOMEM. I put those patches in because LLM review flagged it as a
potential issue, and Qu recommended that approach to fix it.

If we're content to leave that problem until we have evidence that it
is one, we can just drop patches 1 and 2. The later patches don't have
any dependencies on them.

Dave, would that resolve your concerns?

-ENOMEM abort analysis from the LLM for anyone interested:
---------------------------8<--------------------------

  btrfs_orphan_add aborts by errno:                                   
                                                                                                                  
  ┌────────────┬────────┬───────┐                                     
  │   errno    │ events │ hosts │                                     
  ├────────────┼────────┼───────┤                                     
  │ -5 EIO     │ 131    │ 127   │                                     
  ├────────────┼────────┼───────┤                                     
  │ -28 ENOSPC │ 1      │ 1     │                                     
  ├────────────┼────────┼───────┤                                     
  │ -12 ENOMEM │ 0      │ 0     │                                     
  └────────────┴────────┴───────┘                                     
  Same result with the cascade filter dropped (293 events / 270 hosts, all -5).                                   
                                                                                                                  
  Three controls make that a real negative rather than a query artifact:                           

  1. ENOMEM aborts exist — 475 events / 471 hosts in the same window, so the query would find them.
  2. The signature is detectable and the code is live — the identical abort site in btrfs_orphan_add: fires for 270 hosts with -5. And btrfs_orphan_add() passes ret straight to btrfs_abort_transaction() with no remapping, so a -12 would print as -12.                     
  3. The path is hot — in the base tree btrfs_orphan_add() is called from btrfs_unlink() (nlink→0), btrfs_rmdir(), btrfs_create_new_inode() (O_TMPFILE), and btrfs_rename() (victim nlink→0). That allocation runs on essentially every file deletion fleet-wide.                 

Where the ENOMEM aborts actually are (hosts/30d): btrfs_rename 147, convert_free_space_to_extents 116, btrfs_add_link 67, convert_free_space_to_bitmaps 56, btrfs_replace_file_extents 42, btrfs_create_new_inode 16.

-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
